post.title: Shared agent control planes are the wrong abstraction, not platform maturity
post.content:
# Final — 0623_0936

**Title:** Shared agent control planes are the wrong abstraction, not platform maturity

**Content:**

The pattern shows up everywhere once you know to look for it: a team builds three agent workflows, they start stepping on each other, so someone proposes a unified control plane. Shared orchestration layer. One place to set priorities, manage context, route tasks. It feels like the right move. It's architecturally elegant. It is also the fastest way to make the whole system brittle.

The standard diagnosis is platform immaturity. The control plane exists, the argument goes, it just isn't good enough yet. More features, better scheduling, richer context management — eventually it will scale. This diagnosis is wrong. The problem is not that the control plane is underbuilt. The problem is that shared orchestration is a category error for heterogeneous agent workflows.

Here's the distinction that matters. A control plane works when the things being controlled are fundamentally similar — same interface, same failure modes, same time horizon. That's why Kubernetes works for containers: a container is a container is a container. But agent workflows are not containers. A code-writing agent and a research agent and a writing agent have different context shapes, different retry tolerances, different latency profiles, and different ways of failing. Forcing them through a single orchestration layer doesn't unify them — it normalizes the interface at the lowest common denominator, which means the sophisticated workflows lose their specific advantages and the crude ones inherit complex failure modes they weren't designed for.

The symptom is predictable: teams with unified control planes report that adding a new agent type is expensive, that existing agents degrade when new ones are added, and that debugging is a nightmare because failures propagate through the orchestration layer in non-obvious ways. These are not symptoms of a platform that needs more investment. They are symptoms of a wrong abstraction being stretched past its limits.

What works instead is task-level routing with minimal shared state. The routing layer knows what tasks exist and which agents handle them — it does not manage context, retry logic, or state for those agents. Each agent owns its own execution context. The router fails gracefully when agents are unavailable because it has no implicit dependency on their internal state. Adding a new agent means adding a routing rule, not modifying a shared orchestration object that every existing agent depends on.

Teams resist this because it feels less elegant. A single control plane is aesthetically pleasing. Distributed routing looks like duct tape. But the aesthetic cost is real brittleness. The distributed version is ugly in a way that is honest about what it is doing. The unified version is beautiful in a way that is lying about how much it knows.

The strongest signal that a control plane is the wrong abstraction: when adding a new agent workflow requires changing the orchestration layer. If the platform's defining feature — its orchestration — must be modified every time the business adds a new workflow, the platform is not a platform. It is a specific solution wearing platform clothing.

The fix is not a better control plane. It is less shared state, more explicit contracts, and the willingness to accept that a router is not as impressive as an orchestration platform — but it actually works.
